330.title: The good of all
330.hook: the year ends where every Ardas ends, asking good for everyone
330.howItsDone: Every Ardas, in every gurdwara and at home, ends with the line asking for chardi kala and sarbat da bhala, the good of all, before the congregation calls out the jaikara.

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at the depths: the Granth's themes, the Bhagats, history and grief, and your line, deep water, crossed. Next to last day of the year: today ends where every Ardas ends.

Amritsar, the 1700s, a spring morning at Vaisakhi. Riders come in from every direction: bands that spend the rest of the year scattered, sometimes quarreling, often hunted. For a few days they camp side by side, sit together before the Guru Granth Sahib, and decide things as one. That gathering, which you met on day 289, was the Sarbat Khalsa. Sarbat, everyone. Everyone who belonged. Every Ardas still ends with that word, but there it reaches far past the riders camped at Amritsar.
screen: `AMRITSAR, VAISAKHI, THE 1700S.` → `THE SARBAT KHALSA GATHERS.` → `THE SAME WORD, REACHING FURTHER.`

segments.voice: On day 251 you took the Ardas's last line apart: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhane sarbat da bhala. Rising spirits through the Name, and, by your will, the good of all. Today, one word, because you've now met it twice. Sarbat. In the Sarbat Khalsa, it meant the whole Khalsa: every band, every leader, everyone who belonged, gathered before the Guru Granth Sahib. In the Ardas, it stretches past every border. Not the whole Khalsa. The whole of everything. Sarbat da bhala: the good of all, full stop. Think who says it. This year's path walked through a community hunted in the forests, massacred in 1746 and again in 1762, turned away from a harbor in 1914, attacked in its holiest place and in its own neighborhoods. The Ardas remembers much of that. And it doesn't end with protect our own, or defeat our enemies. It ends by asking good for everyone, and Sikh teachers often say plainly that this includes the people who did the hurting. It grows out of what the Gurus taught: one light in every person; no enemy and no stranger, as Guru Arjan sings on Ang 1299. And notice tere bhane, by your will. The prayer doesn't tell God what everyone's good should look like. It asks, and leaves the shape of it to the Giver. A fitting place to stand at the end of a year of stories, practices, the Japji and the depths: a prayer whose last word reaches past the people saying it.
screen: `SARBAT KHALSA: THE WHOLE KHALSA.` · `SARBAT DA BHALA: THE WHOLE OF EVERYTHING.` · `A HURT PEOPLE ASKS GOOD FOR ALL.` · `BY YOUR WILL, IN YOUR WAY.` · then, large: `FOR EVERYONE, NOT JUST US.`

segments.voice: Wish good for three people from this year: first someone who taught you something, in any way at all; then someone on the other side of a disagreement you're in, at home, at work or in the news, even a little; last, someone far away whose story you heard on this path and will never meet. Wish each well, in your own words or none. If you pray, hold all three in your prayer; if not, just hold them.
Sarbat. Everyone, the whole of everything — in sarbat da bhala, the last words of every Ardas, asking good for all.
Your line: for everyone, not just us. Sarbat da bhala. Day three hundred thirty.

331.title: The big lookout
331.hook: year one is done; ahead lie the ranges: the daily banis, the long story, the ways of the Guru, the Granth itself
331.howItsDone: Sikhs often describe themselves as lifelong learners of the Guru, and the Ardas said at the close of gurdwara gatherings ends by asking for chardi kala, rising spirits, and the good of all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sarbat: every Ardas ends by asking good for everyone, and your line, for everyone, not just us. Today, the lookout.

Near the top of a long hike, tired legs earn a stop. A hiker turns around, and there it is: the whole valley walked through, small and golden below. Then the other way: more mountains, bigger ones, blue in the distance. Two thoughts can arrive at once: I made it, and look how much more there is. This is that spot, the last day of year one.
screen: `A TIRED HIKER TURNS AROUND.` → `THE VALLEY BEHIND, SMALL AND GOLDEN.` → `MORE MOUNTAINS AHEAD.`

segments.voice: Start with the word Sikh. It's usually traced to an old Indian word for a student, a disciple, a learner. Sikhs often put it simply: a Sikh is someone who keeps learning from the Guru, not someone who finishes. So a year doesn't end with a diploma; it ends at a lookout. Turn around first. You began with first words: seva, Waheguru, Ik Onkar, langar, sangat. Then the stories: ten Gurus, one light. Then the practices: kirtan, simran, Nitnem, a visit to the gurdwara. Then the Japji, pauri by pauri, all thirty-eight and the saloks. Then the depths: the Granth's great themes, Kabir and Farid, the rehat, the history, and the grief of 1984 carried carefully. That's the valley. Now face the other way. Four ranges. First, the daily banis: Jaap Sahib tomorrow, then Anand Sahib, Rehras, Kirtan Sohila, Sukhmani, the prayers many Sikhs say morning and evening. Then Sikh history, told slowly, century by century. Then the ways of the Guru, lived day to day. And then the Granth itself, fourteen hundred thirty pages, the Guru Sikhs bow to. Daunting? Sikhs have a phrase for the spirit to meet it with, from day seventeen: chardi kala. Rising spirits, an unbeaten, upward-facing mind. It sits in the Ardas's last line, right beside yesterday's good of all. Chardi kala isn't pretending things are easy. The Sikh story has plenty of hard days, and this year's path passed through some of them. It's facing forward anyway, in good heart, because the road is long and the company is good. That's the lookout: grateful behind, awake ahead.
screen: `SIKH: A LEARNER WHO KEEPS LEARNING.` · `THE VALLEY: WORDS, STORIES, PRACTICES, DEPTHS.` · `THE RANGES: BANIS, STORY, WAYS, GRANTH.` · `CHARDI KALA: FACE FORWARD, IN GOOD HEART.` · then, large: `WOW.`

segments.voice: Find a window and let your eyes go as far as they can: a rooftop, a tree, a strip of sky. Breathe slowly and think back over one word, one story, one practice that stayed with you this year; then let your gaze go to the edge of what you can see, and notice there is more out there. If you pray, you can say Waheguru under your breath, the Sikh word of wonder from camp one; if not, simply stay with what you see.
Chardi kala. Rising spirits, an unbeaten, upward-facing mind — the spirit to meet the ranges ahead, the banis and the Granth, at the top of year one.
Your line: wow. For a sky, a kindness, a sentence that lands. Year one, done.

332.title: The Tenth Guru's morning praise
332.hook: Jaap Sahib is a rolling litany of the Timeless One's qualities, said each morning after Japji
332.howItsDone: Sikhs who keep Nitnem recite Jaap Sahib each morning, right after Japji Sahib, often from memory or from a small prayer book (gutka).

segments.voice: Yesterday, chardi kala: the valley of year one behind you, the ranges ahead, and your line, wow. Today, year two begins with the first range, the daily banis.

What do people do when one sentence isn't enough? Listen to a best man at a wedding. He doesn't say, my friend is good. He says: loyal, ridiculous, the one who drove four hours at midnight, the one who still remembers your mother's birthday. Love turns into a list. The list speeds up. Everyone laughs, and somebody cries. Sikhs have a morning prayer built just like that, a list that keeps going, faster and faster, because no single word will do. It comes right after Japji.
screen: `ONE SENTENCE ISN'T ENOUGH.` → `LOVE TURNS INTO A LIST.` → `THE LIST SPEEDS UP.`

segments.voice: Its name is Jaap Sahib. Jaap comes from jap, to repeat, to recite, the same root as japna, the steady repeating of the Name. Sahib is a word of respect, the way Sikhs honor a bani. So the title means something like: the honored recitation. Sikh tradition credits it to Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru. It isn't in the Guru Granth Sahib; it opens a second collection, the Dasam Granth, the book linked with the tenth Guru. In the standard text it runs to one hundred ninety-nine stanzas, and almost all of it is names: qualities of the Timeless One, line after line. Many begin with a small sound, a, which means without. Without form. Without birth. Without fear. Without end. It praises by saying: whatever you picture, it's more than that. The language is a rich mix: mostly Braj, an old poetic Hindi, with words shaped like Sanskrit, and passages in Persian, full of Persian and Arabic words. The meter keeps changing, chhand after chhand, some stately, some so quick the words drum. The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, lists the morning banis: Japji first, Guru Nanak's quiet wisdom; then Jaap, the Tenth Guru's praise; then ten short verses called the Tav Prasad Savaiye. The first Guru and the tenth, side by side every morning. Japji thinks. Jaap sings, and keeps moving. Over the next thirty days, it unfolds a few names at a time.
screen: `JAAP: TO REPEAT, TO RECITE.` · `THE TENTH GURU, 199 STANZAS.` · `A: WITHOUT FORM, WITHOUT BIRTH, WITHOUT END.` · `JAPJI FIRST, THEN JAAP.` · then, large: `PRAISE AT PACE.`

If you can't play anything, listen to the sounds around you, one after another, without naming them. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once at the end.

333.title: No mark, no caste
333.hook: the opening stanza says He has no mark or sign, no color, caste or lineage (Jaap 1)
333.howItsDone: Sikhs who keep Nitnem recite this opening stanza every morning as the start of Jaap Sahib, and the Gurus' rejection of caste is lived out in langar, where all sit in one row, and in the shared Khalsa names Singh and Kaur.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jaap Sahib, the Tenth Guru's morning praise, and your line, praise at pace. Today, its very first stanza.

A conference badge: name, company, job title, maybe a little colored dot for vegetarian. Within two seconds of meeting someone, you've read it, and they've read yours. Plenty of life runs on marks like that. Accent, neighborhood, last name, the logo on a shirt: little marks that tell everyone where to put you. In the Tenth Guru's Punjab the marks were sharper still: caste, clan, the sign painted on a forehead, the cut of a robe. And the Tenth Guru opens his great praise by taking every one of those marks and saying: none of these apply.
screen: `A BADGE: NAME, COMPANY, TITLE.` → `MARKS THAT TELL US WHERE TO PUT PEOPLE.` → `JAAP OPENS: NONE OF THESE APPLY.`

segments.voice: The first stanza of Jaap begins with a list of absences. Its opening words, chakr chihan ar baran jaat ar paat nahin jih, mean roughly: the One who has no mark and no sign, no color, no caste, no lineage. Chakr is a mark, the kind of sign some religious groups wore to show which god or sect they followed. Chihan is any sign at all. Baran is varna, the old word for the great classes of Indian society, and it also means color. Jaat is caste. Paat is lineage, the family line. In the Guru's world, these labels decided who could eat with whom, marry whom, learn which texts, enter which temple. The stanza goes on: form, complexion, outline, dress, nobody can describe them. So before Jaap praises a single quality, it clears the table. Whatever badge you would pin on the Divine, take it off. Here's why that lands for Sikhs. The Gurus had been taking those same badges off people since Guru Nanak. Langar, where everyone sits in one row and eats the same food. Sangat, where anyone may sit before the Guru. And tradition says that when he founded the Khalsa, the Tenth Guru gave its members shared names, Singh and Kaur, so a surname could no longer announce a caste. Some Sikhs hear the opening of Jaap and the founding of the Khalsa as one idea from two sides: the One has no caste, so the people who bow to that One shouldn't wear caste either.

You don't have to answer; if you pray, you can say Waheguru once, softly.

334.title: King of kings
334.hook: He is called king of kings and lord of countless Indras (Jaap 1)
334.howItsDone: Sikhs bow their foreheads to the floor (matha tekna) before the Guru Granth Sahib in the gurdwara, and often speak of the Guru as sachcha patshah, the true king.

segments.voice: Yesterday, no mark: the One with no sign, no caste, no lineage, and your line, no mark, no sign. Today, the same stanza turns from what He isn't to what He rules.

Delhi, in the Tenth Guru's lifetime. The emperor holds court, and his titles take a full breath to read aloud. Among them is a Persian one: shahanshah, king of kings. Courtiers bow to the floor. Coins carry his name. Far to the north, in the hills, a Guru is writing a hymn. And in its very first stanza he takes that same title, king of kings, and gives it away. Not to any man on any throne.
screen: `DELHI: AN EMPEROR HOLDS COURT.` → `SHAHANSHAH: KING OF KINGS.` → `A GURU GIVES THE TITLE AWAY.`

segments.voice: After the list of absences, the first stanza of Jaap turns. The One is achal moorat, an unmoving form; self-lit, of boundless power. Then a line with two great titles. Kot indr indraan: lord of millions of Indras. Saahu saahaan: king of kings. Start with Indra. In the old stories of India, Indra is the king of the gods, ruler of a shining heaven, the one who sends the rain. Lord of a single Indra would already be enormous. Jaap says millions: every heaven anyone has pictured, each with its own crowned king, and the Timeless One above them all. Then saahu saahaan, the same title the emperors carried in Persian. In one line the Guru gathers the highest ruler of the old Indian heavens and the highest ruler of the Persian-speaking courts, and sets both below the One. Why does that matter? As Sikhs read it, a person who believes there is a King above every king stands differently in front of power. Sikhs call the Guru sachcha patshah, the true king, and bow their heads to the Guru, to the Guru Granth Sahib, not to thrones. Sikh history remembers people who would not bow where their conscience said no, and who paid for it. The line isn't a protest slogan. It's praise. But praise like this changes posture. If the One is above every throne, every throne on earth is borrowed. In that reading, a head bowed to the One in the morning need not bow to fear.

335.title: Named by deeds
335.hook: no one can tell all His names; the wise name Him by His works (Jaap 1)
335.howItsDone: Sikhs use many names for the Divine, Waheguru, Akal Purakh, Gobind, Kartar, and many of them, like Kartar (the Creator) and Dayal (the Merciful), are names drawn from what the One does.

segments.voice: Yesterday, patshah, lord of millions of Indras, and your line, above every throne. Today, the last two lines of that first stanza, and a question: if the One has no mark, what do you call Him?

Every apartment building has them: neighbors whose names you never learned. So you name them by what they do. The guy who waters the plants at six. The woman who always holds the elevator. The kid practicing trumpet, badly, with total commitment. You don't know who they are on paper. You know them by their deeds, and that might be the truer name. The first stanza of Jaap Sahib ends on exactly this idea.
screen: `NEIGHBORS WHOSE NAMES YOU NEVER LEARNED.` → `THE ONE WHO HOLDS THE ELEVATOR.` → `KNOWN BY WHAT THEY DO.`

segments.voice: The first stanza has stripped away every label: no mark, no caste, no form anyone can draw. It has called the One king of kings. Now, its last two lines. First the whole of creation speaks: gods, humans, demons, even the forests and the grass, and what they say is net net. Not this, not this. It's a very old phrase in Indian thought, for a reality so large that every description has to be refused. Then the question the stanza has been building to: who can tell all Your names? Nobody. And the answer: the wise speak Your karam naam. Karam means deeds, works, actions. Naam means name. Names drawn from what You do. That's the hinge of the whole hymn. Everything Jaap is about to say, salutation to the Merciful, to the Protector, the Giver, the Destroyer of cruelty, these are deed-names. Not a passport. A list of what the One has been seen to do. Guru Arjan says something close in the Guru Granth Sahib, on page one thousand eighty-three: the tongue speaks names made from Your deeds, and Sat Naam, the true Name, is Your name from before all beginnings. So Sikhs hold two things together. There's a Name beyond all naming. And there are countless names that come from noticing: mercy here, protection there, a gift that arrived on time. The wise, Jaap says, don't argue about the first. They keep a record of the second.
screen: `NET NET: NOT THIS, NOT THIS.` · `WHO CAN TELL ALL YOUR NAMES?` · `KARAM NAAM: NAMES FROM DEEDS.` · `ANG 1083: DEED-NAMES AND SAT NAAM.` · then, large: `NAMED BY DEEDS.`

segments.voice: Name one thing you've seen the Divine do, or, if that language doesn't fit you, one thing life did for you that you didn't arrange: a recovery, a stranger's help, a morning that came after a terrible night. Give it a deed-name, the way Jaap does, the one who sent help, the one who kept me, and breathe with it. If you pray, you can say it with Waheguru; if not, let it simply be a thank-you.
Karam naam. Names drawn from what the One does: no one can tell all the One's names, so the wise name Him by His works.
Your line: mercy here, protection there. The names come from noticing. Three hundred thirty-five days, and counting.

336.title: The snake's gait
336.hook: the next stanzas move in a meter named for a snake's gliding motion
336.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the bhujang prayat stanzas of Jaap Sahib in a steady, rolling rhythm, often quickly and from memory, and in a group the shared meter keeps everyone together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, karam naam: no one can tell all His names, so the wise name Him by His works, and your line, mercy here, protection there. That ended Jaap's first stanza. Today, the hymn changes its walk.

Watch a snake cross a path. It doesn't step. It doesn't hop. It pours. A small ripple starts at the head and travels down the whole body, and the snake is somewhere else before you've decided whether to be scared. No jerks, no pauses, one smooth wave after another. Indian poets heard that motion in certain rhythms of words, and they named one meter for it. When Jaap Sahib leaves its first stanza, it starts to move exactly like that.
screen: `A SNAKE CROSSES THE PATH.` → `IT DOESN'T STEP. IT POURS.` → `A RHYTHM NAMED FOR THAT MOTION.`

segments.voice: The meter is called bhujang prayat. Bhujang is a snake; prayat means going, moving. The snake's gait. It's an old meter of Sanskrit poetry, and Guru Gobind Singh uses it for long stretches of Jaap. It's built from little groups of three syllables, and every group goes the same way: short, long, long. Da, DUM, DUM. Listen to the opening of the second stanza: na-mas-tvam, a-kaa-le. Short, long, long. Short, long, long. Then: na-mas-tvam, kri-paa-le. And: na-mas-tvam, a-roo-pe. Then: na-mas-tvam, a-noo-pe. Once you hear it, you can't stop hearing it. Each group is a small wave, and the waves keep rolling, line after line, the way a snake's body carries one ripple into the next. Why does rhythm matter in a prayer? Because Jaap is meant to be said out loud, often fast, often from memory, often by a whole room together. A steady meter lets a whole room glide through salutation after salutation without losing its place. The rhythm carries the words, so the mind is free to carry the meaning. And that ends the week. A few days ago you stood at the lookout. Since then: Jaap, the Tenth Guru's morning praise; the One with no mark and no caste; the king of kings above every throne; and the names drawn from deeds. Now the hymn begins to glide.
screen: `BHUJANG: SNAKE. PRAYAT: GOING.` · `SHORT, LONG, LONG: ONE SMALL WAVE.` · `NAMASTVAM AKAALE, NAMASTVAM KRIPAALE.` · `THE RHYTHM CARRIES THE WORDS.` · then, large: `GLIDE.`

segments.voice: Say four lines slowly, tapping your knee on each long syllable: namastvam akaale, namastvam kripaale, namastvam aroope, namastvam anoope. Say them once more, a little faster, and let them run together like one long wave; the meaning comes over the next few days. Then stop, and let your breath find its own smooth rhythm, no jerks, no pauses.
Bhujang prayat. The snake's gait: a meter of short, long, long waves that Jaap Sahib glides in for long stretches.
Your line: glide. The rhythm carries the words. Day three hundred thirty-six: a week, done.

screen: `DAY 336 COUNTS.` → `A WEEK OF JAAP BEGUN.` → `TOMORROW: SALUTATION TO THE TIMELESS.`
